questions.q: Why is this lesson's mock session a genuinely different exercise from Lesson 8's first mock session, rather than a repeat?
options: Because it uses a completely different presentation format never seen before
Because Lesson 8 did not actually involve a case study at all
Because this lesson requires a live audience of at least ten people

Because it comes after the full Chapter 2 and 3 toolkit (assumptions, risk prioritization, blueprint artifacts, rejected alternatives, objection patterns), testing whether that toolkit can actually be applied, not just whether the format is understood
questions.explain: Lesson 8 tested whether the candidate understood the presentation format; this lesson tests whether the full set of tools built across Chapters 2 and 3 can actually be used together under time pressure.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend choosing a case study you haven't already used in an earlier mock session?
options: Because drilling the same scenario twice teaches performing that specific scenario well, not applying the method freshly, which is the actual skill being tested
Because reusing a case study is against the course's terms of use
Because each case study can only legally be presented once
Because a fresh scenario is always technically simpler than a repeated one
questions.explain: The point of this exercise is testing the method on unfamiliar material, the same reasoning Lesson 9 used for applying the requirements-extraction technique to a brand-new scenario.

questions.q: What intermediate artifacts does this lesson say should actually be produced before building the timed presentation outline, unlike Lesson 8's lighter run-through?
options: Only a cost estimate and a staffing plan
A requirements breakdown, stated assumptions with consequences, a prioritized risk list, the four blueprint artifacts, and at least one honestly-justified rejected alternative
A single, fully detailed field-level data dictionary and nothing else
A marketing slide deck summarizing the case study for an external audience
questions.explain: This session is meant to actually produce the full chain of artifacts from Lessons 9 through 13, not skip straight to the presentation the way the lighter Lesson 8 exercise did.

questions.q: Why does this lesson ask for at least one predicted question from each of the three objection-pattern families (data/security, integration/scale, delivery/governance)?
options: Because panels are contractually required to ask exactly three questions
Because only one objection family is ever actually tested in a real review board
Because deliberately covering all three families guarantees the mock session doesn't accidentally skip an entire category of challenge just because it felt less natural to write
Because the three families must always be asked in a fixed order
questions.explain: Without deliberately drafting from all three families, a candidate's self-generated questions tend to cluster around whichever type feels most natural, leaving real gaps untested.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does "harder" mean for this second mock session, as opposed to picking an artificially more complex scenario?
options: Holding yourself to the full standard from every lesson so far at once — stated assumptions, fair rejected alternatives, protected Q&A pacing, and reasoning-based answers to planted objections
Choosing a scenario with more pages of text than any Chapter 1 case study
Presenting without any preparation time at all
Requiring a panel of at least five people instead of one
questions.explain: Every Chapter 1 case study already touches multiple domains; 'harder' here means applying the complete toolkit rigorously, not picking a more complicated story.
